abstract: How does learning a spatial context shape the selection of a newly salient distractor? In two eye-tracking experiments (26 participants each), observers searched for a T among Ls in repeated (Old) or novel (New) configurations. A designated distractor occupied a fixed or variable location and became a red color singleton in the second session. Repeated configurations predicted a stable target location in Experiment 1 but not in Experiment 2. Familiar configurations yielded faster responses alongside an increased probability of initial saccades toward fixed-location singletons. These co-occurring effects were observed at outer singleton locations in Experiment 1 and at both inner and outer locations in Experiment 2. Contextual cueing was stronger in Experiment 1, where familiar configurations also increased initial target selection, reduced ordinary-distractor selection, and facilitated target acquisition. These findings suggest that learned context shapes both the priority assigned to individual search items and search efficiency following distractor selection. The singleton probe reveals how learned spatial contexts shape both the distribution of attentional priority across individual search items and the efficiency of search following distractor selection.
